title: Detraining: Loss of Training-Induced Physiological and Performance Adaptations. Part I: Short Term Insufficient Training Stimulus
population: Trained athletes and recently trained individuals; short-term (under 4 weeks) insufficient training
findings: Short-term detraining (under 4 weeks) in highly trained athletes brings a rapid decline in VO2max and blood volume; exercise heart rate does not rise enough to offset lower stroke volume, so maximal cardiac output falls.
Ventilatory efficiency and endurance performance are impaired; changes are more moderate in recently trained individuals.
Metabolically: greater carbohydrate reliance (higher exercise RER), lower lipase activity, GLUT-4 content, glycogen level and lactate threshold.
Muscle: capillary density and oxidative enzyme activities are reduced; fibre cross-sectional area gains reverse, but strength performance declines are limited.
limitations: Narrative review from 2000; the abstract gives no quantified rates and the review is not run-specific.
implications: Model fitness loss as starting within the first 2-4 weeks of no or low training: reduce the starting load after a 2-4 week layoff and re-estimate threshold paces rather than using pre-break paces.
Strength is lost more slowly than aerobic capacity, so strength sessions can resume closer to previous loads than running volume.

verification.notes: Own re-fetch: Crossref title (Part I), Sports Medicine 2000, Mujika first author, 2 authors. All findings in abstract. Removed unsupported 'mostly men' limitation claim.
